vakbeschrijving.nl:
Exploring the Grand Challenges is part of the Applications, Impact and Skills as well as the Earth System Data learning line, and sets the scene for the type of problems Earth, Climate and Technology students may end up working on. You will explore the grand challenges linked to relevant Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and discover the relevance of what you will learn in the programme to be able to come up with solution pathways from the perspective of Earth, Climate and Technology.  

The course revolves around a data-driven approach: by selecting readily available online datasets (e.g., on population, climate, energy use and production, biodiversity, economy) you will explore the grand challenges, and at the same time learn how to analyse, synthesise and present data. These skills will be built on in the course Geodata Fundamentals, where you will learn the essential ingredients of the data-to-insight workflow: problem formulation – data requirements and acquisition – processing, analysis, evaluation – interpretation and communication. 

Exploring the grand challenges is intertwined with a computer literacy and coding classes, in which you will learn the fundamentals of programming (incl. use of loops, functions, numpy, matplotlib, pandas) and apply exploratory data analysis to summarize and visualize the main characteristics (e.g., variability, correlation, distribution, uncertainty) of spatial and temporal data related to the grand challenges. 

Towards the end of the course, you will pick one challenge to study in more detail as a group project. 

In terms of skills, we will help you to get settled into the university environment and develop critical thinking skills. This includes aspects such as study planning, looking at problems from an engineering perspective and teamwork. The course will include classes on writing, presenting, academic standards (referencing, fraud, plagiarism, use of artificial intelligence) and ethical work practices. Through workshops and the group project, you will also develop skills such as social and personal skills, and presentation skills.  

Portfolio 
Throughout the programme, you will work on your portfolio. The objectives are to let you think about the relevance and relations between the courses, learning lines, and disciplines; and to reflect on your personal and academic development. A template of the portfolio will be provided, which includes assignments that are related to the skills training within the Applications, Impact and Skills courses.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
This course is an introduction to the Principles of the Earth and Climate System from a global perspective. It presents the composition, dynamics and interaction of Earth’s spheres: geosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, biosphere and anthroposphere; with a larger emphasis on the first two. The rock, water and carbon cycles will be examined with conceptual or simple models to illustrate some of these interactions. The contemporary Earth and Climate System will be related to its (geological and preindustrial) past and to the different possible futures. The course provides a comprehensive perspective that will be used in following semesters as a framework to guide the application of technology to the monitoring, exploration, use and preservation of Earth’s resources (geothermal, wind and solar energy, minerals, safe climate, clean air, soil and water). 

Specific topics include the origin of the Earth, geodynamics, elements, minerals and rocks, the rock cycle, geological time scales, the coupled evolution of Earth’s subsurface, surface and atmosphere, and an introduction to the present-day atmosphere, oceans and cryosphere, and the effects of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions on the climate.  Water transport over the surface and through the subsurface, rivers, lakes and oceans will be introduced (to be followed up in the following semester). The Climate System will be studied with a focus on natural and anthropogenic influences, the basics of the greenhouse gas effect and the effect of internal feedbacks, and an introduction to the models used to assess possible future climates.  Atmospheric topics include the vertical structure of the atmosphere, global energy balance, basic thermodynamics, and an introduction to global circulation (winds). Ocean topics include an introduction to spatial variations in temperature and salinity, basic processes for sea-ice and the wind-driven and thermohaline circulations (currents). For the carbon cycle, the long-term and present-day budgets will be discussed, including the sources and sinks of natural and anthropogenic carbon.

leerdoelen.nl:
1. Characterize the main processes of all spheres of the Earth and climate system (geosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, biosphere) (ILO1,2)

  2. Explain short- and long-term interactions between Earth’s spheres with a focus on the rock, water, and carbon cycles (ILO1, 8) 

  3. Describe the evolution of the Earth System through the Earth history at geological to human time scales in view of the character and functioning of its main spheres (ILO4) 

  4. Use simple numerical models to explain the effects of natural and human factors on the Earth and climate system (ILO1,3, 8) 

  5. Identify different types of minerals and rocks and explain their origin (ILO4) 

  6. Explain the causes and effects of contemporary and past climate change (ILO6)

  7. Explain how  future climates projections are constructed through the use of climate models, the design of representative emission scenarios, and inputs from observational data  (ILO8) 

In summary: ILOs1-4, 6, 8

(Part A, 4EC): 

  • Written exam on Rock and minerals lab (40%)  

  • Mid-term written exam (60%) in week 1.9  on the contents from weeks 1.1 to 1.8. Topics included are geosphere (5/8 of exam), atmosphere (2/8 of exam), and climate system (1/8 of exam)

  • Final written exam  (closed book) (100%) in week 2.6 on the contents from weeks 1.10 to 2.4. The topics that will be examined are:

    • geosphere (1/5 of exam),

    • ocean, glaciers, vegetation in the Earth System, carbon cycle, future climate (3/5 of exam)

    • interactions between spheres of the Earth System (1/5 of exam).

It presents the composition, dynamics and interaction of Earth’s spheres: geosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, biosphere and anthroposphere; with a larger emphasis on the first two. The rock, water and carbon cycles will be examined with conceptual or simple models to illustrate some of these interactions. The contemporary Earth and climate system will be related to its (geological and preindustrial) past and to the different possible futures. The course provides a comprehensive perspective that will be used in following semesters as a framework to guide the application of technology to the monitoring, exploration, use and preservation of Earth’s resources (geothermal, wind and solar energy, minerals, safe climate, clean air, soil and water). 

Specific topics include the origin of the Earth, geodynamics, elements, minerals and rocks, the rock cycle, geological time scales, the coupled evolution of Earth’s subsurface, surface and atmosphere, and an introduction to the present-day atmosphere, oceans and cryosphere, and the effects of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions on the climate.  Water transport over the surface and through the subsurface, rivers, lakes and oceans will be introduced (to be followed up in the following semester). The Climate System will be studied with a focus on natural and anthropogenic influences, the basics of the greenhouse gas effect and the effect of internal feedbacks, and an introduction to the models used to assess possible future climates.  Atmospheric topics include the vertical structure of the atmosphere, global energy balance, basic thermodynamics, and an introduction to global circulation (winds). Ocean topics include an introduction to spatial variations in temperature and salinity, basic processes for sea-ice and the wind-driven and thermohaline circulations (currents). For the carbon cycle, the long-term and present-day budgets will be discussed, including the sources and sinks of natural and anthropogenic carbon.

1. Characterize the main processes of all spheres of the Earth and climate system (geosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, biosphere) (ILO1,2)

  2. Explain short- and long-term interactions between Earth’s spheres with a focus on the rock, water, and carbon cycles (ILO1, 8) 

  3. Describe the evolution of the Earth System through the Earth history at geological to human time scales in view of the character and functioning of its main spheres (ILO4) 

  4. Use simple numerical models to explain the effects of natural and human factors on the Earth and climate system (ILO1,3, 8) 

  5. Identify different types of minerals and rocks and explain their origin (ILO4) 

  6. Explain the causes and effects of contemporary and past climate change (ILO6)

  7. Explain how  future climates projections are  constructed through the use of climate models, the design of representative emission scenarios, and inputs from observational data  (ILO8) 

In summary: ILOs1-4, 6, 8

vakbeschrijving.nl:
This course will introduce the basic concepts of Newtonian Mechanics and Thermodynamics.  

Mechanics is the study of the motion of bodies under the action of physical forces.  The course will focus on the conditions for static equilibrium, on the motion of particles and rigid bodies, and on the motion and deformation of continuums such as solids, fluids and gases.  Thermodynamics is the study of how energy can be converted in different forms by applying heat and work.  This course will examine how the macroscopic properties of continuums change under the influence of heat, work and mixing in terms of their temperature, volume and state of aggregation. 

The relevance of mechanics and thermodynamics is first discussed at theoretical and basic level whereafter it is applied and illustrated by analyses of many relevant mechanical and thermodynamical processes that take place in the solid earth, the oceans, the cryosphere and the atmosphere. These applications will illustrate and motivate the usefulness of mechanics and thermodynamics for Earth, Climate and Technology.  

In addition to the specific knowledge acquired, students will also practice how to conceptualise physical problems and solve them by making use of first principles and the fundamental physical laws of mechanics and thermodynamics.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
This course consists of two parts:

  1. Part 1: Functions of multiple variables

  2. Part 2: Differential equations

In Part 1, we extend the student's knowledge of calculus applied to functions depending on one variable to functions depending on two or more variables.

We focus on the operations of differentiation and integration applied to such functions.

In addition, the student's "mathematical toolbox" will be expanded with techniques for working with vectors, taking derivatives and performing integration.

Topics in Part 1 are among others

  • Vectors, inner product, cross product;

  • Equations of lines and planes;

  • Inverse trigonometric functions;

  • Differentiation and integration techniques;

  • Functions of multiple variables;

  • Partial and directional derivatives;

  • Extreme values of functions;

  • Multiple integrals;

  • Coordinate systems.

In Part 2, we focus on differential equations. These are needed during the modeling of physical phenomena in the study of the earth and climate.

We focus on solving some specific types of differential equations.

Topics in Part 2 are among others

  • Complex numbers;

  • Direction field;

  • First and second order differential equations;

  • Taylor polynomials.

leerdoelen.nl:
After a successful completion of this course the student should be able to:

  1. compute the dot and cross product of two vectors and use this in other computations;

  2. set up parametric and cartesian equations for lines and planes in three-dimensional space;

  3. determine the domain of a function of multiple variables and compute its partial derivatives and tangent planes;

  4. determine the gradient of a function of multiple variables, describe the gradient geometrically, use the gradient to compute tangent planes and directional derivatives and solve optimization problems;

  5. compute multiple integrals;

  6. decide whether it is beneficial to use polar, cylindrical and spherical coordinates to compute double and triple integrals and perform these computations;

  7. set up a mathematical model to describe engineering problems using differential equations (DEs);

  8. interpret a direction field;

  9. solve first order linear and separable DEs;

  10. use DEs to model vibrating springs;

  11. solve second order linear DEs with constant coefficients;

  12. approximate solutions to DEs using Taylor polynomials.

Examination dates and Examination method

  • For each part, there is optional homework in Grasple which is part of a bonus regulation;

  • For Part 1, the exam is at the end of Period 1;

  • For Part 2, the exam is in the middle of Period 2;

  • The resit for Part 1 and for Part 2 is at the end of Period 2;

Examination will be administered digitally in a secured environment on a computer in a PC hall at the TU Delft. To participate in an examination, the student needs to be present in the scheduled PC hall. Every examination consists of a written component.

In case the examination cannot be administered in the digital format with written component, then the entire examination will be in a written format.

Permitted materials during examination

During each examination of this course, the student may use the following permitted materials.

Permitted materials which the student is responsible for:

  • Pen and pencil;

  • Ruler, protractor triangle (geodriehoek) and compass.

Other permitted materials which is provided at the examination:

  • Formula sheet (https://prime.pages.ewi.tudelft.nl/formula-sheets/AESB1211/AESB1211.html);

  • Scrap paper;

  • Answer form for the written component.

Other materials are not permitted. This includes the following:

  • Calculator;

  • Pencil pouch;

  • Smart devices (including mobile phones, smart watches);

  • Own notes.

These materials should not be present on the table and should be stored.

To receive a final grade for this course (ECTB1140), the student needs to meet the following criteria:

  • For Part 1, a grade of minimum 5,0 (not rounded to wholes and halves) is earned;

  • For Part 2, a grade of minimum 5,0 (not rounded to wholes and halves) is earned;

If both the criteria is met, then the student will receive a final mark, computed as the average of the grades for Part 1 and Part 2.

The final mark will be rounded to wholes and halves. The student passes the course if the final mark is minimum 6,0 (after rounding to wholes and halves). The least average for passing the course is 5,75 (not rounded).

vakbeschrijving.nl:
This course provides an in-depth introduction to the dynamic interactions between the Earth's subsurface, surface, and atmosphere and the role of water in these interactions. It integrates key concepts from geomorphology, hydrology, and atmospheric sciences, offering students a comprehensive understanding of the physical processes that shape landscapes, control water distribution, and influence climate and weather patterns.

In the surface section (Geomorphology), students will explore landform development, erosion, sediment transport, and the impact of tectonic activity on the Earth's surface. Attention is given to the role of glaciers, hillslopes, rivers, wind, and coastal processes in shaping natural environments.

In the water section (Hydrology), we will explore the hydrological cycle at global and local scales. Students will develop a comprehensive understanding of the water and energy balance at the surface, precipitation climatology and extremes, unsaturated flow and infiltration, evaporation, groundwater, runoff generation and streamflow. Students will analyze hydrological data and apply modeling techniques to diagnose and predict the spatial and temporal characteristics of water storage and fluxes. Attention is given to the role water plays in connecting processes in the subsurface, surface and atmosphere at a range of temporal scales.

 In the atmospheric sciences portion, students will learn about atmospheric structure, and weather systems The course covers topics such as atmospheric turbulence, atmospheric thermodynamics, boundary layer meteorology, and clouds and convection . All this from the perspective of 1D analysis (vertical column) and modelling and where appropriate relate to the surface energy balance including   water and vegetation surfaces and soils (land).

 Through a combination of lectures and practical exercises, students will develop analytical skills to assess environmental processes and their interconnections. By the end, students will be able to evaluate how landforms, water systems, and atmospheric dynamics interact to shape the natural world and respond to environmental changes.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
Geodata Fundamentals brings together knowledge of geophysics and remote sensing, of statistics, and of computer science to lay the foundations for the learning line Earth System Data. Through practical examples, this course will teach you the basic principles behind making informed decisions under uncertainty to manage subsurface resources, mitigate geohazards, or predict future weather and climate, among other applications. 

Building around the concept of the data-to-insight workflow, you will learn the essential ingredients to acquire, manage, process, analyze, and interpret Earth system data based on two main parts: 

  1. In this first part (Sensing and Statistics), you will focus on the principles behind Earth system data acquisition and analysis. Uncertainty is inherent to studying and managing Earth systems, so you will start with an introduction to important concepts in probability and statistics. Then you will learn about Earth system data acquisition using a selection of geophysical and remote sensing techniques.

  2. In the second part (Applied Statistics with Python), you will focus on the practical use of statistics to start extracting meaningful insights from Earth system data using Python. Here you will learn to clean, transform, and analyze data and to build statistical models to predict properties related to Earth systems. You will work on case studies using the data you acquired yourself during the first part and data from other sources.

At the end of this course, you will have gone through the entire data-to-insight workflow based on an initial selection of data acquisition and analysis techniques. In the following courses of the learning line Earth System Data, you will progressively build your knowledge towards more specialized or advanced techniques, for instance to tackle the specificity of time series and spatial data, which are ubiquitous around Earth systems.

toelichting_onderwijsmethode.nl:
This course focuses on an inquiry- and case-based learning approach. Throughout the course, you will be introduced to several case studies comprising an open question and one or several Earth system datasets that you need to analyze – and acquire for some cases – to answer the question. Guidance around the different steps needed to tackle each case study and their implementation in Python will be progressively reduced, so that, by the end of the course, you can manage a case study by yourself just based on a question and a dataset. 

Contact hours are divided between interactive, practical, and Q&A sessions: 

  • Interactive sessions consist of a mix of theory and practice, where a specific case is used as the basis for Earth system data acquisition, processing, or analysis. vakbeschrijving.nl:
Geodata Fundamentals brings together knowledge of geophysics and remote sensing, of statistics, and of computer science to lay the foundations for the learning line Earth System Data. Through practical examples, this course will teach you the basic principles behind making informed decisions under uncertainty to manage subsurface resources, mitigate geohazards, or predict future weather and climate, among other applications. 

Building around the concept of the data-to-insight workflow, you will learn the essential ingredients to acquire, manage, process, analyze, and interpret Earth system data based on two main parts: 

  1. In the first part (Sensing and Statistics), you will focus on the principles behind Earth system data acquisition and analysis. Uncertainty is inherent to studying and managing Earth systems, so you will start with an introduction to important concepts in probability and statistics. Then you will learn about Earth system data acquisition using a selection of geophysical and remote sensing techniques.

  2. In this second part (Applied Statistics with Python), you will focus on the practical use of statistics to start extracting meaningful insights from Earth system data using Python. Here you will learn to clean, transform, and analyze data and to build statistical models to predict properties related to Earth systems. You will work on case studies using the data you acquired yourself during the first part and data from other sources.

At the end of this course, you will have gone through the entire data-to-insight workflow based on an initial selection of data acquisition and analysis techniques. In the following courses of the learning line Earth System Data, you will progressively build your knowledge towards more specialized or advanced techniques, for instance to tackle the specificity of time series and spatial data, which are ubiquitous around Earth systems.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
Chemistry for Earth Sciences will extend what you know from chemistry in high-school to what you need as an engineer in Earth, Climate & Technology. The topics that are addressed in this course are taken from aqueous chemistry, geochemistry, mineralogy, atmospheric chemistry and environmental chemistry. The content covers both equilibrium and non-equilibrium reactions in homogeneous phase systems (liquid, solids, gas), as well as reactions in heterogeneous systems containing mixtures of solids, liquids and gases. In these heterogeneous systems, reactions across interfaces are important. The course is based on a quantitative approach where the underlying mathematics are important so that students can understand and apply these concepts in a modeling framework. 

The content will expand the knowledge from high-school on acid-base chemistry, redox-chemistry, chemical thermodynamics, phase-diagrams, equilibrium and non-equilibrium chemistry, and the understanding of chemical compounds to the context of earth sciences.

3.1

Introduction to chemistry for the earth system 

The story of this course starts with the origin of all elements. We will discuss the composition of the galaxy, the solar system, and the earth. Where did the elements come from and what is their distribution on Earth? And why is chemistry so important for understanding the processes governing the Earth System?   
The Earth system consists of the: Atmosphere; Hydrosphere; Lithosphere and the Biosphere. Each with a specific composition.  
In discussing these topics we will revisit the theory of the structure of the atom, the periodic table of elements, and the types of chemical bonding.   

3.2 

Lectures (2 x 1 hours)  
Formative assessment (1x 0.5 hour, exam level)  
Self study (6.5 hours)  
Excercise practicals (2 x 1.5 hours)  

Single phase aqueous chemistry; activity and chemical potential 

Reactions in water are central to the chemistry of the earth. This week we will revisit concepts you have had in high school, but we will put them in to the perspective of Earth Sciences.  
The topics addressed will include: mass action law; Gibbs free energy; activities; chemical potential; chemical equilibria; equilibrium constant; chateliers principle; standard conditions (both chemist's and biochemist's). The aim of the week is to develop the mathematical equations describing these concepts which are foundational for the the Earth, Climate and Technology programme. 

3.3 

Lectures (2 x 1 hours)  
Formative assessment (1x 0.5 hour, exam level)  
Self study (6.5 hours)  
Excercise practicals (2 x 1.5 hours)  

Multiphase chemistry, heterogeneous reactions across interfaces: gas-liquid and liquid-gas. 

This week we will focus on the interactions between water and the other phases on earth: gases and solids. The aim is to extend the mathematical foundations so that we can include reactions with and in the other phases. 
Topics that will be addressed are : partial pressures; activities of solids; fugacity; solubility products; Henry's law; Raoults law; solid solutions and the concepts of reversible and irreversible adsorption (clays, organic matter and oxides) 
  

3.4 

Lectures (2 x 1 hours)  
Formative assessment (1x 0.5 hour, exam level)  
Self study (6.5 hours)  
Excercise practicals (2 x 1.5 hours)  

Electrochemistry, redox chemistry 

In week 4 we will discuss redox reactions (reduction-oxidation reactions), an important class of chemical reactions involving the transfer of electrons between molecules. Redox reactions play fundamental roles in e.g. the cycling of elements through the Earth system, and it is important to have a solid understanding of the key concepts. In this week, you will learn how to calculate the oxidation state of molecules, how to formulate the overall reaction equation from the electron donor and acceptor half reactions, or from only the donor and acceptor molecules, and calculate the standard potential for chemical as well as biological standard conditions. You will explore the importance of redox reactions to the Earth System by diving more deeply into the (bio)geochemical cycling of a specific element (e.g. C, N, S, P, O, Fe, …) through different redox states and the main processes mediating their cycling between these states.   

3.5 

Lectures (2 x 1 hours)  
Formative assessment (1x 0.5 hour, exam level)  
Self study (6.5 hours)  
Excercise practicals (2 x 1.5 hours)  

Modelling chemistry with software packages 

In order to be able to work with realistic systems, we need to use computer models. This week you will be introduced some of the essential concepts in modelling (geo)chemical problems. We will first focus on equilibrium models. 
Many of the assignments in the course have a computer model underlying the calculations. After this week you should be able to setup some problems for your self.

Lectures (2 x 1 hours)  
Formative assessment (1x 0.5 hour, exam level)  
Self study (6.5 hours)  
Excercise practicals (2 x 1.5 hours)  

Atmospheric examples 

In weeks 6 – 8 we will apply the fundamentals and tools you learned in weeks 1 – 5 to real world examples. We will dive into the chemical processes impacting the atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water) and geosphere (solids), with a special emphasis on anthropogenic factors. Examples could include the formation of acid rain, changes in groundwater quality due to human activity, the oxidation of metal sulfide ore deposits at mining sites, and the formation and precipitation of carbonate sediments in marine environments.

In this week you will start to understand why equilibrium processes are the exception on earth. Life on the planet can only exist as a consequence of non-equilibrium. Non-equilibrium is driven by the transformation of energy of the sun and the earth itself!

Redox reactions play fundamental roles in e.g. the cycling of elements through the Earth system, and it is important to have a solid understanding of the key concepts. In this week, you will learn how to calculate the oxidation state of molecules, how to formulate the overall reaction equation from the electron donor and acceptor half reactions, or from only the donor and acceptor molecules, and calculate the standard potential for chemical as well as biological standard conditions. You will explore the importance of redox reactions to the Earth System by diving more deeply into the (bio)geochemical cycling of a specific element (e.g. C, N, S, P, O, Fe, …) through different redox states and the main processes mediating their cycling between these states.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
Linear Algebra is a branch of mathematics which is based on two mathematical operations: addition and (scalar) multiplication. Despite this deceptive simplicity, it has a vast variety of applications, both within and outside mathematics. 
 
This course is an introduction to several fundamental aspects of Linear Algebra, like vector calculation, solving systems of linear equations and matrix algebra, and notions like linear combinations, linear (in)dependence, linear transformations, subspaces, bases, dimension, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalisation, standard inner products, and orthogonal projections.

vakbeschrijving.nl: This course integrates theory and skills obtained in other courses in a real-world field setting. You will discuss properties, processes and links between different parts of the Earth system in a field setting, based on your own observations and measurements. The course revolves around a trip along the Meuse river, between the Belgian Ardennes and the Dutch Limburg. Before the trip, you will prepare for the excursion by collecting information and analyzing data from the field area. In the field, you gain real-world experience with topics related to the subsurface, surface, water, (paleo)climate and weather, as well as with relevant measuring techniques. The field trip itself consists of two components. First, in an excursion-style field trip, you will learn to observe and measure various components of the Earth system through exercises at excursion stops. Then, in a group project, you will focus on acquiring data, e.g. river discharge, geophysical measurements, GNSS profiles and a LiDAR based DTM. After the field trip, you and your group will process, analyze, visualize and interpret this data, and present your findings to other groups in a poster session.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
The subsurface is a key element of the Earth System. It contains natural resources (ores, geothermal heat, water), provides temporary and permanent storage (CO2, heat and cold, H2, and nuclear waste) and influences engineering operations conducted in, close to, or on the surface. Understanding the natural and engineered conditions of the subsurface is essential for a safe and sustainable future. The subsurface domain is challenging because it is hard to directly observe. Its behavior needs to be derived from fundamental physical and geological laws and by predictive models occurring across various spatio-temporal scales. A comprehensive understanding of the subsurface requires a multidisciplinary approach, integrating insights from Earth sciences (Principles of Earth Science learning line) and geodata science (Earth System Data learning line).

Plate tectonics is the fundamental framework driving our understanding of geological structures and processes. The course kicks off by contextualizing the subsurface’s significance for society, relating topics such as geo-energy, subsurface storage, geo-resources, and how infrastructures interact with the shallow subsurface and how geo-hazards relate to tectonic settings.

We then examine how tectonics influence the formation and evolution of sedimentary basins, showing the evolution from the deposition of sediments to their transformation (lithification) into rocks. In this part of the course, the students will also learn about the impact and occurrence of earthquakes and volcanism related to different tectonic settings and stages of basin evolution. They will develop conceptual geological models enhancing their ability to think in 2D, 3D and 4D, while connecting theory to real-world applications.

We finish the course by introducing geological heterogeneities and their impact on the subsurface processes. Different scales and types of heterogeneity (sedimentary, structural, mechanical and chemical) will be described and related to the physical processes from which they originate. Students will discuss how heterogeneity and uncertainty are related, and how they impact our ability to safely and sustainably engineer subsurface applications. Throughout the course students will explore techniques from micro- to macro-scale for acquiring subsurface data in a range of practical exercises.

vakbeschrijving.nl: This course will focus on understanding how the global-scale motions of the atmosphere and ocean govern weather and climate. Students will learn about phenomena such as the jet stream in the atmosphere and the overturning circulation in the ocean, along with fundamental theory that helps explain how these features arise. The theory will introduce students to fluid dynamics affected by Earth’s rotation, and will be illustrated using laboratory experiments, observations and simulations. The concept of variability in the climate system will be introduced and connected to changes in large-scale oceanic and atmospheric flows. Linkages will be established between global climate patterns and consequences at more regional scales, including flooding and extreme heat events. The relevance of these mechanisms in regulating changes in our climate system will be elucidated.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
In the process from data to insights, as the central theme in the Earth System Data learning line, the role of this course lies in taking first steps in exploratory univariate data analysis in time and frequency domain, discovering patterns, features and artifacts, and attempting to describe characteristics of the observed phenomenon or process.

In this semester, students will learn, from an engineer's perspective, to apply signal analysis and processing techniques to one-dimensional datasets. The basic theoretical concepts of Fourier Series and Fourier transform in continuous time are covered, to allow for signal decomposition in the frequency domain. An introduction is given into linear time-invariant systems, convolution and signal filtering, all from a continuous-time perspective. Then discrete time signals are addressed, elaborating on sampling and finite measurement duration, and turning the Fourier transform into the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) for practical application. In the second part of this course, noise is introduced, leading to random processes, first in continuous time, addressing auto- and cross-covariance. Elementary noise processes (such as white noise) are covered, as well as the aspect of stationarity. Then random sequences (in discrete time, i.e. time series) are elaborated upon, covering data interpolation, smoothing and filtering. Finally, students will learn how to construct appropriate, basic models for time series and explore functional relationships and stochastic dependencies. This course aims to convey the theoretical concepts, yet also offer extensive hands-on training, by means of examples, exercises and practical assignments, the latter including also numerical signal and time series analysis in Python with simulated, actual and even live data in class.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
Physical objects are described in a quantitative way with the aid of mathematics. In classical physics, all physical objects are geometric objects. The course “Fields and Waves” combines the physics of fields and waves with the mathematical tools required to describe these phenomena. The course enables students to develop essential understanding of the physical interpretation of mathematical formulations.

The physical meaning of basic mathematical operations, gradient, divergence, and curl are discussed where they occur in physical problems relevant to ECT problems. The topics discussed are gravity and electric potential fields as examples of potential fields (elliptic equations), heat and mass transfer and fluid flow, electromagnetic diffusion (parabolic equations), acoustic, electromagnetic and elastic waves (hyperbolic equations). These fields and waves are used in the ECT domain to probe the Earth's atmosphere, surface, and subsurface with engineering applications in mind.

While being able to find solutions for some specific cases is an important part of the course, the emphasis of the course is on learning how to describe the relevant physics with the corresponding mathematical tools, to understand the solution space, and to be able to give a physical interpretation of the solutions.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
The course Fluid Dynamics covers the essential aspects of both fluid flow, and heat and mass transfer at an introductory level, offering you a starting point for your future careers where insight into processes in atmosphere, ocean, and solid earth are essential.

First, we will look at the basic principles of fluid flow, starting with the different processes that influence flow and combining them into the conservation equations for mass and momentum. From here, we will then treat laminar flow, where attention will be paid to specific examples, including Hagen-Poiseuille flow, Couette flow and Darcy’s Law. Afterwards, non-dimensional analysis and dimensionless numbers are introduced, and the topic of turbulence is explored briefly. Subsequently, attention is focused on heat transfer and the equation for the conservation of energy is derived. Covered subjects include balances for simple heat-transfer problems and different transport mechanisms for heat transport, for example, heat conduction, convective heat transfer, and radiation.

During the course, the strong link between education and recent research/realistic practice in engineering will be emphasized. This will be done by giving examples from realistic geophysical flows: hydrological, atmospheric, oceanic, and subsurface applications.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
All Earth, Climate, and Technology processes, interventions and related challenges are embedded in society. Engineering solutions for a more sustainable society (e.g., wind turbines or batteries, water barriers) require processes that have implications for the Earth and climate system (e.g., greenhouse gasses, ecological impacts). Likewise, changing climatic conditions (e.g., rising temperatures, increasing drought frequencies and geohazards) have impacts on society (e.g., lowering urban liveability, increasing food insecurity).

In this course, you will take challenges (e.g., for the energy transition, for climate mitigation) from stakeholders and explore the connectivity between proposed solutions and society. You will explore, analyse, and reflect on stakeholder requirements, societal needs, and the ethics of various choices, with the results communicated to others. First-hand interaction with stakeholders and exposure to a broad selection of case studies will give context and inform critical reflection on engineering solutions. Lectures and exercises -- centered around i) stakeholder consultation, ii) environmental impact assessment and life cycle assessment, iii) ethics, social responsibility, and data integrity, and iv) critical thinking -- will provide a new range of skills which can be applied to Earth, Climate, and Technology challenges.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
This course bridges the theoretical Earth System knowledge acquired in the previous Principles of Earth System courses with practical applications in subsurface engineering. It explores how Earth science principles underpin engineering activities in various parts of the subsurface, including: 1) the upper 50 meters of the subsurface relevant to geotechnical engineering, 2) the deeper subsurface, used for water and heat extraction, energy storage, and waste disposal, and 3) critical raw material extraction at any depth. The course emhasises the Earth Science aspects of these engineering applications, focusing on a) methods for characterising subsurface properties, b) the nature and implications of geoscientific uncertainties, and c) the relative importance of geoscientific aspects in the engineering application at stake. There is attention for, but less emphasis upon, the engineering aspects of the applications and the dynamic behavior related to the engineering, which are part of other courses of the BSc and, particularly, the more specialized tracks in the EC&T MSc. At this stage, the students will learn about how Earth System theory and practice is needed for engineering in the subsurface.  

The course is organised into three main components:  

  1. Predictability of the subsurface characteristics and the related uncertainty 

This part builds directly on the preceding Earth Subsurface course, which introduced the character and variability of the subsurface.  . This will be continued here focusing on the predictability of these heterogeneities and their related uncertainty.  

2. Characterisation of Earth subsurface properties 

This component addresses methods for investigating and quantifying subsurface properties. Topics include geophysical and petrophysical methodologies, cores and cuttings as direct subsurface sediment and rock samples, and shallow subsurface methodologies such as Cone Penetration Tests. Last, upscaling of properties in geomodelling will be discussed. 

3. Impact of Earth subsurface character on engineering applications 

Here, students integrate knowledge from the first two components to explore how subsurface characteristics influence subsurface engineering applications . This relates to the dynamic response, uncertainty propagation, project efficiency, and project safety. 

Given the broad scope of the subject, the course cannot cover all topics in equal depth. Instead, selected topics and applications are explored in detail to help students understand the complete workflow from data acquisition to engineering interpretation. Other topics are introduced through overview lectures to provide broader context. The selected case studies are aligned with examples from other BSc courses, ensuring that students gain both a comprehensive overview of the field and a foundation for specialisation in the MSc tracks. 

Lecture topics are complemented by hands-on practical exercises and project work to allow students to get to know the data, materials, and techniques actively. Alignment with the Data Learning Line is made to work on similar data and data analysis techniques. 

The course concludes with a summative written examination.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
In this course, you will explore the rapidly changing Earth system as it responds to human activity over the past and current century. Building on concepts that you have learnt about the principles of the Earth system in the first year, in this course, you will focus on modern anthropogenic climate and environmental change, its mechanisms, impacts and subsequent implications for living systems.

You will investigate how key components of the climate system, i.e. the atmosphere, ocean, land, carbon and biosphere interact under the influence of human-induced forcing. You will go from understanding global-scale trends to assessing their regional and local impacts, such as extreme heat and precipitation, sea-level rise, ice melt, wildfires and biodiversity loss. Along with understanding these impacts, you will also understand cross-cutting concepts such as uncertainties, tipping points, compound events and the challenge of comparing models with real-world observations, all of which are highly relevant to the discussion of the aforementioned topics.

This course will have a major part which uses a hands-on approach. Through guided computational exercises using platforms like KNMI Climate Explorer and Climate Reanalyzer, you will learn to analyze climate datasets, interpret model outputs, and assess patterns in both mean and extreme events. You will develop practical skills in evaluating climate projections (from global and regional simulations) while learning the coupling of atmosphere, land, ocean and carbon systems in a warming climate.

This course will emphasize understanding and application over memorization and hence, we have short, analytical assignments throughout the course with a final project that links data interpretation to contemporary climate issues. By the end, you will be equipped to critically analyze ongoing climate and environmental change shaping our planet today by bridging concepts from theory and data.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
The goal of the course is twofold. First, students will learn to work with new sensing techniques from earth observation and geophysics that extend their knowledge from Year 1. These techniques include multispectral and seismic imaging techniques. Second, after this course, students will have obtained the knowledge and skills to critically derive information from uncertain 2D Earth System data.  

Students will get acquainted with the concept of spatial analysis and students will be trained in acquisition, processing, and analysis of 2D Earth System data.  Building on the fundamentals acquired in previous courses of the Earth System Data learning line (Grand Challenges, Geodata Fundamentals, Signals and Time Series), students will advance their skills towards notably imaging systems and two-dimensional datasets.  

 Image acquisition systems provide spatial data that varies in terms of coverage and volume, quality, and complexity.  In the Sensing and Spatial Analysis course, students will learn to work with processing techniques to estimate variable properties and the uncertainties in these estimates at a given spatial location. These processing techniques incorporate spatial variability, data uncertainty and scales in different ways and include deterministic and stochastic interpolation, 2D Fourier analysis, supervised and unsupervised classification, and spatial filtering and smoothing.  

Students will use the different spatial processing methods on data from known and newly introduced sensing techniques. Students will notably learn about principles and properties of multispectral remote sensing and geophysical data, while students will apply spatial analysis techniques on known sensor data such as   meteorological data, GNSS, photogrammetry and laser scanning. Students will learn to use QGIS and Python as tools to work with realistic scenarios of spatial analysis using data sets consisting of thousands to millions of observations.  

This course is directly related to the 2nd years Fieldwork Project, that runs in the same semester. Students will process multispectral remote sensing data in the Fieldwork Project using methods introduced in this course.

[LO2] Apply spatial analysis techniques in an efficient workflow on real spatial data of various data types using a GIS system and Python.

[LO5] Estimate uncertainty of spatial measurements and derived parameters.

[LO6] Differentiate between different spatial analysis methods of interpolation, classification, smoothing and filtering in terms of computational efficiency, robustness, ease of use and quality of results.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
This course introduces students to the essential mathematical "building blocks" and techniques required to solve systems of equations, which play an important role in many practical applications across the earth sciences.

We will introduce the numerical methods used for modelling natural earth system phenomena (e.g. ground water flow, ocean circulation and atmospheric flow) and induced responses (e.g. seismic wave propagation). The students will work on simplified simulation approaches for the governing equations underlying these subjects. These governing equations will represent the many processes that are at play in the Earth systems.

We will first connect the governing equations in the context of different applications in earth sciences and explain the principles of discretization in time and space. Students will learn how different choices in discretization in space and time influence the accuracy and reliability of numerical results. Beyond applying numerical methods, students will design workflows that move from describing an earth system process, to formulating the governing equations, and finally to implementing and interpreting numerical simulations. This will help them relate their simulation outcomes back to the original scientific problems.

Foreseen topics included in the course are:

  • overview of different systems of coupled equations and fields of application

  • the “Why” from continuous world to discrete representation

  • numerical integration

  • numerical interpolation

  • discretization methods for partial differential equations (1D, 2D..) application to diffusion, advection, wave and/or Laplace equations, potential fields

  • numerical optimization

  • high performance computing

vakbeschrijving.nl:
In this course, students acquire a fundamental basis for one- and two-phase flow in porous media. This course is an essential basis for all tracks within the MSc Applied Earth Sciences as well as the MSc track in Geotechnical Engineering in the MSc Civil Engineering. This course is highly recommended for students interested in Hydraulic Engineering as well as Hydro-geology and Water Management.

The course will address the following topics:

  • basic principles for groundwater flow under saturated conditions (1D, 2D and 3D, both stationary as well as non-stationary flow);

  • (potential) energy and its relationship with pressure and head;

  • capillary pressure and unsaturated flow (2-phase flow in a porous medium filled with water and air);

  • concepts of water and air content, saturation, hydraulic conductivity, relative permeability, and residual saturation;

  • water retention curves (van Genuchten, Brooks-Corey, and Gardner equations);

  • the impact of flow on soil mechanics, highlighting the connection with the parallel course of soil mechanics.

vakbeschrijving.nl:
Basics of log evaluation and introduction to measurements on rock. Practical laboratory work on porosity, permeability, capillarity, parameter determination of rock, principles of acoustic, electric, electro-magnetic and nuclear measurements in boreholes, identification of water and hydrocarbons, quantification of reservoir properties. 

Lectures and exercises: 
Introduction to the identification, measurement and use of physical rock parameters. Rock mineral content and rock textures, of mainly sedimentary rocks, are related to properties like density, conductivity, magnetics, (natural/induced) radiation, acoustics and rock mechanics.

In relation to the reconstruction of a synthetic mineral content, methods to derive porosity, permeability and capillarity are discussed and calculated in practicals. The practical work consists of five ways to measure permeability/porosity and to determine rock mechanical properties by using a combined acoustic/stress experiment.

Details:
1. Laboratory measurement: Darcy-flow and porosity.
A. Experiments at the Geoscience and Engineering Laboratory. This work includes measurements on solid and porous cores. Measured are: Bulk volume and bulk weight and the related matrix volume and matrix density; Calculation of the porosity on the two porous samples, with a dry method and the wet/dry method; Calculation of the gas-permeability of the two porous samples; Estimation of the measurement errors and calculation of the accuracy of the measurements. 
B. Combined acoustic and rock mechanical measurements. Uni-axial stress is put on a solid core. Different types of acoustic waves are used to measure travel time through the undamaged and fractured rock specimen. Elastic moduli are calculated from both measurement types.


2. Empirical relations. 
A. Carman-Kozeny permeability. Based on spatial distributions of a porous rock texture, porosities and permeabilities are calculated by using statistical spatial characteristics, i.e. grain size distributions, derived volumes and specific surfaces. 
B. Quantification of grain sizes and grain-size distributions, by using rock surfaces and images.
In this exercise the students get familiar with the concept of empirical relations. How are grain-size distribution, porosity, permeability and capillarity connected to each other? 


Well log measurement principles and data processing and interpretation through petrophysical models. Indirect measurements to estimate physical parameters are outlined for the most important well logs. Petrophysical models for resistivity, density and seismic velocity are introduced and related to the log measurements. Exercise on synthetic and real logs are carried out to apply petrophysical model to data integration and quantitative log interpretation.

Petrophysics:

1.     Fluid conductivity and effect of temperature, salinity and pressure. Archie’s Law and its modification for shaly sand formations

2.     Solid and fluid mechanical properties. Willye and Gassmann models for monomineral materials, fluid substitution. Voight-Reuss average for multimineral media. Effect of porosity and mineralogy on those properties

Logs:

1.     General concepts about logs: investigation depth and resolution. Mud invasion, caliper logs

2.     Lithology logs: Self potential and Gamma ray, measurement principles, corrections and data quantitative interpretation. Shale volume estimation

3.     Resistivity logs, laterolog, focalized tools and induction log measurements and data correction. Water saturation estimate.

4.     Neutron and Density logs: measurement principles and data corrections. Estimate of porosity through Neutron-Density cross plot.

5.     Sonic logs: measurements principles, porosity estimation.

6.     Image logs: measurements principles and bedding azimuth and dipping estimation.

7.     Log lithological interpretation and fluid recognition from integration of different log measurements. Case study presentation.

Synthetic log exercise: autonomous work to retrieve the petrophysical properties from a synthetic log dataset. The quantitative analysis of the different logs allows rock and fluid properties to be retrieved and porosity models to be identified.

Field log interpretation exercise: unsupervised work on real log data to carry out lithology identification, fluid identification, estimation of shale volume, porosity, water saturation.

leerdoelen.nl:
The student is educated on the essentials regarding interpretation of rock type/mineralogy, related rock physical properties and rock textures. This to define its mineral/fluid composition and geological/mechanical properties. The student learns how to measure and interpret rock characteristics. Finally, they learn to do a standard log evaluation on clastic sediments. The obtained experience is beneficial for the Field Exploration Project (AESB3440) in Period 4.

At the end of this course, the student can quantify rock masses and images:
- interpret rock types and mineralogy
- understand the underlying rock physics and is able to recognize rock textures. 
- use multiple methods of measuring rock properties
- measure and interpret rock characteristics using laboratory instruments and dedicated software. 
- perform a simple log evaluation of clastic- and bio-sediments using standard logs. 
- complete a digital log evaluation and several types of laboratory tests, both alone and in groups.

vakbeschrijving.nl: Climate change is one of the dominant global long-term trends affecting the work of the Applied Earth Sciences engineer. It impacts the boundary conditions of coastal defence systems, off-shore engineering, water management and large infrastructure design. Optimal risk management and long-term sustainability are only possible when the potential consequences of climate change are taken into account. Not only mitigation and adaptation, but also the science behind climate change is an engineering problem, with several open-standing questions to solve. This course provides students with the current scientific knowledge of the climate system, of climate change, and the role of processes in the atmosphere, land and ocean in climate change. Furthermore, students will gain experience in the interpretation of climate variability and global and regional climate change relevant to engineering challenges.

toetsing.nl:
The thesis:
The student writes a report referred as Bachelor Thesis. The report is assessed by an assessment committee composed of the certified supervisors. Additional members can join the assessment committee and grade the student if they comply with the rules of the Board of Examiners (Art 23 - https://www.tudelft.nl/studenten/faculteiten/citg-studentenportal/onderwijs/onderwijsinformatie/educational-rules-and-regulations). If additional members do not comply with the rules of the Board of Examiners, they can join the deliberation as advisor, but they are not grading the student.

The final Bachelor Thesis must be uploaded on OnStage at least two days before the defense to be checked for plagiarism (turn-it in, requirement to be checked in Brightspace Bachelors Graduation Project Manual). The student must upload the receipt into OnStage, as well as a self-reflection.

The defense:
Before the end of week 9 of each quarter or of week 5.2 for the students following the FEP in Q4, the students defend their BEP research in front of the assessment committee. The defense presentation is completed by the student using a visual support (power point). The duration of the presentation is limited to 15 minutes. Each presentation is followed by 15 minutes of scientific questions about the performed research from the audience and assessment committee. After the defense it is of the responsibility of the student to upload her/his Bachelor Thesis presentation into OnStage

The students research is judged following six rubrics: research approach (10%), profoundness (30%), evaluation of the results (20%), organization (5%), written report (25%) and oral presentation (10%). The description of the various categories is available upon request.

The Bachelor Thesis and the Bachelor Thesis defense are assessed independently following the same rubrics. The final grade is an average of the thesis (written) and presentation (oral) grade. No specific weighting is applied.

The rubrics with the motivation of the judgement must be signed by the reviewers and uploaded by the supervisor(s) at the end of week 9 at the latest (or at the end of week 5.2 in Q4 for the student having completed their FEP). The results are then uploaded into Osiris

vakbeschrijving.nl:
Central to this course is data collection in the French regional parc of the ‘Baronnies Provençales’ (in the Drôme Region). In teams of three, you will prepare, execute, and report on an Application-Driven Project based on a Field Survey. In short, you are given a ~50km2 area in the southeast of France for you and your team to do fieldwork so that you collect – bottom to top – scientific data to solve a scientific and/or engineering problem.

Before the field work, there will be two weeks of preparation in Delft. During these weeks, your time will be dedicated to equipping you with solid field-based workflows to characterise the geosphere (geology), the atmosphere (atmosphere observations) and everything in between (hydrosphere and biosphere; Remote sensing). In the second preparation week, you will also get training for a specific Application-Driven Project (ADP).  The outcome of this second preparation week is the plan of your field campaign that combines field-based technologies, methods, and workflows. 

During field work (weeks 4.6, 4.7, and 4.8), you start with general field activities, which we call the ‘Field Survey’ and aim at having you characterising the Earth’s spheres with a focus on the geosphere. You do that by following the scientific method. In all phases of your field work, you will be acquiring Earth and Climate data daily, in a systematic manner. 

There, for about one third of your time, you will be conducting specific field activities for your ADP. The “FIELD survey” from your area will feed data to your selected “application-driven PROJECT”, together making your FIELD PROJECT unique. With additional field methods and technologies, you will be able to work on a real problem with your data.

Once you are back to Delft and for two weeks, you will report on your team’s findings about your area and ADP in an oral presentation.

Students with disabilities who cannot participate in the field work would join a team and assist them either from Delft or the field camp.

Field Project = Field Survey + Application-Driven Project (ADP)

toelichting_onderwijsmethode.nl:
Pre-Field Project (First semester and early second semester) 

Logistics: Make teams, book your accommodation, get an area attributed to your team, and arrange for your transportation to – and in – the field work area.   

Preparation phase (2 weeks; 2x40 hours of total time) 

Lectures: Fieldwork Introduction & HSE, available Application-Driven Projects, Sampling method and bias, 

Practical: Geological workflow, GIS/Remote Sensing workflow, Atmospheric workflow, Field reconnaissance, Dunham classification, Geological mapping, and VRock sessions.

Training: Drone training, specific to the ADP (methods & technologies), and HSE Training.

Assignments and deliverables (see details in Assessment forms and moments and weekly descriptions): First through third sets of deliverables. 

  Field work phase (3 weeks; 3x40 hours of total time) 

First Day: 

  • Excursion to familiarize students with geologic, remote sensing, and atmospheric observations.  

Field Activities : 

  • Geology: 1) Find outcrops, 2) characterize outcrops (i.e., surveying of the geosphere from the surface) by gathering data, samples, and following a checklist (e.g., location, dip angle/azimuth, grain size, geomorphologic feature, layering and alternations, structural features, etc...) associating a quality flag/weight to each collected data, 3) Interpret outcrops: based on collected information, make an educated guess about the stratigraphy, sedimentology, and structural geology, 4) test hypothesis by going towards predicted younger or older strata in the stratigraphic series, and 5) repeat while completing the field outcrop (fact) and geological (interpretation) maps. Keep detailed notes in a field notebook.  

  • Remote Sensing: 1) Identify different type of land surface components (i.e., surveying of the biosphere, geosphere and hydrosphere from the surface and the atmosphere), 2) classify the land surface by gathering data, samples relating to soil type / vegetation species, geometric and spectral characteristics (including height and surface temperature), coverage and distribution, 3) obtain waypoints and 4) repeat  

  • Atmospheric Observations: Students measure micro-meteorological (i.e., surveying of the atmosphere from the surface) variables (e.g., air temperature, humidity, windspeed, precipitation) both at a centralized and mobile location and observe cloudiness every day (individual fixed location near their starting point). 

  • Application-Driven Project (ADP): field activities will depend on the selected project and will be detailed with the projects offered each year (list of available ADP projects is subject to change each year).  

Camp activities: 

  • Geology: draw structural, outcrop, and geological maps; construct cross sections; write detailed description of outcrops, catalog/archive collected rock samples (sedimentology), encountered rock formations (stratigraphy), and major folds/faults (structural geology); tidy up and back up field notebook; plan geology survey for next day; liaise with neighboring teams.   

  • Remote Sensing: Maintaining a GIS project, collecting training data, and making land cover map.  

  • Atmospheric Observations: review daily weather in comparison to forecast and look at and take note of the forecast for the following day. 

  • ADP: camp activities will depend on the selected ADP and will be detailed with the projects offered (list of available ADP projects is subject to change each year).
